hook: Pretraining data loading is twelve lines of code. Get one index wrong and your model learns to copy instead of predict.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Pretraining data loading is twelve lines of code. Get one index wrong and your model learns to copy instead of predict.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-2, Llama and nanoGPT all train on one giant flat array of token ids. There are no documents and no epochs in the usual sense, just random windows. Why does that work, and how do you read a 2 GB file without loading it into RAM?

1:00 INTUITION — Picture the whole dataset as one long tape of token ids. Every training example is a window of length T cut at a random spot. The target is the same window slid right by one. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — For a start index i: x = tokens[i : i+T], y = tokens[i+1 : i+T+1]. Valid starts are 0 to N-T-1, so sample i ~ Uniform{0, ..., N-T-1}, which is torch.randint(N - T, (B,)). Number of distinct windows is N-T, so with N = 470M TinyStories tokens and T = 256 we will never see the same window twice by accident. Each window gives T next-token predictions, so one batch is B*T training signals, not B.

4:30 CODE — Open the TinyStories train.bin from M04E08. data = np.memmap(path, dtype=np.uint16, mode='r'). Explain uint16: vocab 10000 fits under 65535. def get_batch(data, batch_size, context_length, device): ix = torch.randint(len(data) - context_length, (batch_size,)); x = torch.stack([torch.from_numpy(data[i:i+context_length].astype(np.int64)) for i in ix]); y = same with i+1. Shapes: x and y are (B, T) int64. On CUDA add x.pin_memory().to(device, non_blocking=True); on the Mac just .to('mps'). Show nanoGPT's trick of re-creating the memmap each call to avoid a slow memory growth.

8:00 RECEIPT — assert x.shape == y.shape == (B, T); assert (x[:, 1:] == y[:, :-1]).all(); assert x.dtype == torch.int64; decode x[0] and y[0] with your tokenizer and show y is x shifted by one word piece. Then run the CS336 Assignment 1 test: uv run pytest -k test_get_batch. Expected: 1 passed.

9:30 MEASURE — Time 1000 calls of get_batch(B=32, T=256) on the Mac: batches per second and tokens per second. Compare to the model's training throughput from M06E09 later. The point: the loader is not the bottleneck, by about two orders of magnitude.

10:30 TAKEAWAY — An LM batch is random windows from one flat tape, and the target is the input shifted by one. Interview line: 'I memmap a uint16 token file and sample random offsets, so loading costs nothing and every window is a fresh example.'
11:00 NEXT — Next: Loss and perplexity
key_math: x = tokens[i : i+T], y = tokens[i+1 : i+T+1], i ~ Uniform{0..N-T-1}; signals per batch = B*T
code_task: get_batch(data: np.memmap[uint16], batch_size: int, context_length: int, device: str) -> (x, y), both LongTensor (B, T) on device. Memmap the TinyStories train.bin from M04E08.
receipt: assert (x[:, 1:] == y[:, :-1]).all() and x.shape == (B, T); CS336 A1 test: uv run pytest -k test_get_batch passes.
gotchas: Using torch.randint(len(data) - T + 1) lets the last y run off the end by one token; Forgetting .astype(np.int64) leaves uint16 tensors that nn.Embedding rejects; Loading the whole .bin with np.fromfile on a big dataset eats all your RAM, memmap does not
interview_q: Why do LM pretraining pipelines sample random windows instead of iterating over documents? Model answer: Random offsets over a concatenated token stream give an effectively infinite set of distinct, i.i.d.-ish examples with zero padding waste, and memmap makes reading them almost free. Documents are separated by an end-of-text token so the model learns boundaries.
explainer: We start with the whole TinyStories dataset laid out as one long strip of numbered tiles, every tile a token id.
We drop a bracket of width eight at a random spot on the strip. That bracket is one training input, called x.
We copy the bracket and slide it one tile to the right. That shifted copy is the target, called y.
Each tile in x is paired with the tile directly below it in y. That is eight next-token predictions from one window.
Now we drop four brackets at four random spots. Stacked together they make a batch of shape four by eight.
The strip itself never enters memory. Only the bracketed tiles light up, because memmap reads just the bytes we touch.
The headline: one flat file, random offsets, and a shift by one. That is the entire pretraining data pipeline.

hook: Before training, your model's loss should be 9.21 on TinyStories. If it is 40, you have a bug, found with zero GPU hours.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Before training, your model's loss should be 9.21 on TinyStories. If it is 40, you have a bug, found with zero GPU hours.

0:15 QUESTION — Every training run you will ever watch is one number going down: cross-entropy. Karpathy checks the step-zero loss of every GPT he trains. What is that number, why is it ln of the vocab size, and what does perplexity actually mean?

1:00 INTUITION — Cross-entropy is how surprised the model is by the true next token. A model that knows nothing spreads probability evenly over V tokens, so it is as surprised as a fair V-sided die. Perplexity is the size of that die. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Per position: loss = -log p(y | context) = -logits[y] + logsumexp(logits). Average over B*T positions. Uniform prediction p = 1/V gives loss = ln V: ln(10000) = 9.21 for our TinyStories tokenizer, ln(50257) = 10.82 for GPT-2. Perplexity = exp(mean loss). Stability: subtract the row max before exp, logsumexp(z) = m + log sum exp(z - m). Bits per byte for cross-tokenizer comparisons: loss / ln 2 * (tokens / bytes).

5:30 CODE — def cross_entropy(logits, targets): logits (B, T, V) -> reshape (B*T, V); m = logits.max(-1, keepdim=True).values; lse = m.squeeze(-1) + (logits - m).exp().sum(-1).log(); nll = lse - logits.gather(-1, targets.view(-1, 1)).squeeze(-1); return nll.mean(). Then build the GPT from M05E14 with vocab 10000, one batch from M06E01, compute the loss before any step.

8:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(cross_entropy(logits, y), F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, V), y.view(-1))). Then on the untrained model: print(loss) gives about 9.2 to 9.3, and math.log(10000) = 9.2103. Also feed logits of 1e4 magnitude to show the naive version returns inf while yours matches F.cross_entropy. CS336: uv run pytest -k test_cross_entropy.

10:00 MEASURE — Show the step-zero loss for two inits: default PyTorch init gives a value near 9.2; a scaled-up output layer (std 1.0) gives a loss far above ln V. Then a reference ladder for TinyStories: 9.21 uniform, the unigram entropy of the training set (compute it from token counts, it is the best a context-free model can do), and the CS336 target region well under 2 after training.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — Loss at step zero should be ln V; anything else means your init or your loss is broken. Interview line: 'Perplexity is exp of the per-token cross-entropy, the effective number of tokens the model is choosing between.'
11:30 NEXT — Next: Adam and AdamW from scratch
key_math: loss = mean_t [ logsumexp(z_t) - z_t[y_t] ]; uniform => loss = ln V (ln 10000 = 9.21, ln 50257 = 10.82); PPL = exp(loss); logsumexp(z) = m + log sum_j exp(z_j - m)
code_task: cross_entropy(logits: (B,T,V) float, targets: (B,T) long) -> scalar, numerically stable with max subtraction; perplexity(loss) = exp(loss). Step-zero check on the M05E14 GPT with V=10000.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(cross_entropy(logits, y), F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, V), y.view(-1))); untrained model loss within ~0.1 of math.log(10000) = 9.2103.
gotchas: Applying softmax then F.cross_entropy double-softmaxes, F.cross_entropy expects raw logits; Comparing perplexity across different tokenizers is meaningless, use bits per byte; Large init on the LM head gives confident wrong predictions and a step-zero loss of 20+
interview_q: Your freshly initialized 50k-vocab model shows loss 11.5 at step 0. Is that fine? Model answer: It should be about ln(50257) = 10.82; 11.5 means the logits are not near uniform, usually an output projection initialized too large. Fix the init before spending compute.
explainer: We see a bar chart of the model's predicted probabilities over the vocabulary. The true next token is highlighted in green.
Loss is the negative log of the green bar's height. Tall green bar, small loss. Tiny green bar, huge loss.
Now we flatten every bar to the same height, one over ten thousand. This is a model that knows nothing.
The negative log of one over ten thousand is 9.21. That is the loss every untrained model should show.
We draw a die with ten thousand faces. Perplexity, exp of the loss, is the number of faces on that die.
As training sharpens the bars, the die shrinks. Perplexity of five means the model is choosing among about five tokens.
So step zero gives us a free bug check: loss should equal log of the vocab size before a single update.

hook: AdamW is twelve lines. Matching torch.optim.AdamW to the last bit took me an extra hour because of where one epsilon lives.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — AdamW is twelve lines. Matching torch.optim.AdamW to the last bit took me an extra hour because of where one epsilon lives.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-3, Llama 3 and nanoGPT all train with AdamW. It also triples your memory: two extra numbers per parameter. What are those numbers, why the bias correction, and why did 'decoupled' weight decay need its own paper?

1:00 INTUITION — m is a running average of the gradient, the direction. v is a running average of the squared gradient, the noise scale. Each parameter takes a step of roughly lr in the direction of m, scaled down where gradients are large or noisy. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Kingma and Ba: m_t = b1 m_{t-1} + (1-b1) g_t. v_t = b2 v_{t-1} + (1-b2) g_t^2. Both start at 0, so early estimates are shrunk toward zero; E[m_t] = (1-b1^t) E[g], hence m_hat = m_t/(1-b1^t), v_hat = v_t/(1-b2^t). Update: theta -= lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps). Adam plus L2 adds lambda*theta into g, so decay gets divided by sqrt(v_hat) and heavily-updated weights barely decay. Loshchilov and Hutter decouple it: theta -= lr * lambda * theta, applied directly. PyTorch order: decay first, theta *= (1 - lr*lambda), then the Adam step. Memory: params + grads + m + v = 16 bytes per parameter in fp32.

6:30 CODE — class AdamW(torch.optim.Optimizer): __init__(params, lr=1e-3, betas=(0.9, 0.999), eps=1e-8, weight_decay=0.01). In step(): with torch.no_grad(), for p in group['params'] with p.grad: state = self.state[p]; lazily init state['step']=0, state['m']=zeros_like(p), state['v']=zeros_like(p). p.mul_(1 - lr*wd); m.mul_(b1).add_(g, alpha=1-b1); v.mul_(b2).addcmul_(g, g, value=1-b2); bc1 = 1-b1**t; bc2 = 1-b2**t; denom = (v.sqrt() / math.sqrt(bc2)).add_(eps); p.addcdiv_(m, denom, value=-lr/bc1). Show the CS336 handout form, alpha_t = lr*sqrt(1-b2^t)/(1-b1^t), theta -= alpha_t m/(sqrt(v)+eps), and explain it is mathematically close but puts eps in a different place.

9:30 RECEIPT — Clone a small GPT twice with the same seed. Train 100 steps, one with my AdamW, one with torch.optim.AdamW(lr=1e-3, betas=(0.9,0.95), eps=1e-8, weight_decay=0.1), same batches. After every step: for p1, p2: torch.testing.assert_close(p1, p2, rtol=0, atol=0) on CPU float64; on float32 expect exact or 1e-7 level agreement. Then uv run pytest -k test_adamw.

11:00 MEASURE — Plot the max absolute parameter difference per step for the torch-order version (zero) versus the CS336 eps placement (tiny but nonzero, growing slowly). Second plot: optimizer state memory, torch.cuda or sum of m.numel()+v.numel() times 4 bytes, equals 2x model size.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — AdamW is per-parameter normalized momentum plus weight decay that is not divided by the gradient scale. Interview line: 'Adam with L2 decays weights in proportion to 1/sqrt(v), AdamW decays every weight at the same rate, which is what you actually want from regularization.'
12:30 NEXT — Next: Learning-rate schedules
key_math: m_t = b1 m + (1-b1) g; v_t = b2 v + (1-b2) g^2; m_hat = m_t/(1-b1^t), v_hat = v_t/(1-b2^t); theta <- theta(1 - lr*lambda) - lr * m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps)
code_task: AdamW(torch.optim.Optimizer) with state m, v, step per parameter; step() follows PyTorch's order (decoupled decay first, eps added to sqrt(v_hat)). Test harness trains two identical tiny GPTs side by side for 100 steps.
receipt: After each of 100 steps, torch.testing.assert_close(p_mine, p_torch, rtol=0, atol=0) in float64 against torch.optim.AdamW with identical hyperparameters; CS336 uv run pytest -k test_adamw passes.
gotchas: Adding eps to sqrt(v) before dividing by sqrt(bias correction) gives a different update than torch, small but it breaks exact matching; Updating p without torch.no_grad() builds an autograd graph through your optimizer and leaks memory; Applying weight decay to LayerNorm/RMSNorm gains and biases, nanoGPT puts only 2D weights in the decay group
interview_q: What is the difference between Adam with L2 regularization and AdamW? Model answer: With L2 the decay term goes through the adaptive denominator, so weights with large gradient variance are decayed less. AdamW applies decay directly to the weights, so the regularization strength is uniform and independent of the learning-rate adaptation.
explainer: We see a single parameter on a bumpy loss curve, and its gradient arrows flicker in size and direction every step.
The first moment m is a smoothed arrow. It averages the flicker into one steady direction of travel.
The second moment v tracks how big the gradients usually are. Big v means a noisy, steep parameter.
The step is m divided by the square root of v. Steep parameters take small steps, flat ones take larger steps.
Early on, m and v start at zero and read too small. Bias correction divides by one minus beta to the t, lifting them back up.
Now weight decay. With L2, the decay arrow also gets divided by root v, so noisy weights hardly shrink.
AdamW pulls decay out of that division. Every weight shrinks by the same factor, lr times lambda, every step.
Our version and PyTorch's then march together, and the difference plot sits at exactly zero for a hundred steps.

A thick orange arrow (m) emerges, smoothly following the average of the jittery arrows.
A purple bar (v) beside the ball grows when arrows are large.
Equation m/sqrt(v) with two balls: steep region small steps, flat region large steps.
Plot of m_t with and without bias correction for t=1..50; corrected curve hugs the true mean.
Decay arrow passes through a sqrt(v) divider and shrinks for the noisy parameter.
Decay arrow bypasses the divider; two parameters shrink at the same rate.
Line plot 'max |mine - torch|' flat at 0 across 100 steps.
short: The RECEIPT beat: 100 steps, difference exactly zero, then the eps-moved version drifting. Caption: 'One epsilon in the wrong place and you no longer match PyTorch.'
yt_title: AdamW from Scratch: bias correction, decoupled decay, matches PyTorch
x_post: Wrote AdamW from scratch and matched torch.optim.AdamW to 0.0 difference for 100 steps. The catch: torch adds eps to sqrt(v_hat), not sqrt(v), and decays before the Adam step. Both matter for exact matching. Code + video:

The interesting part was that the textbook form with alpha_t folds bias correction differently from PyTorch, so eps ends up in a different place. hook: Remove the warmup from a GPT and the loss jumps in the first hundred steps. I will show you exactly where it goes wrong.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Remove the warmup from a GPT and the loss jumps in the first hundred steps. I will show you exactly where it goes wrong.

0:15 QUESTION — GPT-3, Chinchilla and Llama all use linear warmup then cosine decay to about 10 percent of peak. Newer runs like DeepSeek-V3 and the speedrun use warmup-stable-decay. Why warm up at all if Adam already normalizes the step?

1:00 INTUITION — At step one Adam's v estimate is built from one or two gradients, and the network is in its most chaotic state, so a full-size step is a big blind leap. Warmup is easing off the clutch. Cosine decay is braking smoothly into the parking spot. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — CS336 get_lr_cosine_schedule(t, a_max, a_min, T_w, T_c). If t < T_w: a = t/T_w * a_max. If T_w <= t <= T_c: a = a_min + 0.5 (1 + cos(pi (t - T_w)/(T_c - T_w))) (a_max - a_min). If t > T_c: a = a_min. Check endpoints: at t = T_w cos 0 = 1 gives a_max; at t = T_c cos pi = -1 gives a_min. Warmup-stable-decay as a contrast: flat at a_max then a short linear decay at the end.

5:00 CODE — def get_lr_cosine_schedule(t, a_max, a_min, T_w, T_c) -> float. In the training loop: lr = get_lr(...); for g in opt.param_groups: g['lr'] = lr. Plot over 5000 steps with T_w=200, a_max=1e-3, a_min=1e-4. Then an ablation: same tiny GPT on TinyStories, 1500 steps, lr 3e-3, warmup 0 vs 100 vs 300 steps. Log loss and global grad norm per step.

8:30 RECEIPT — Two checks. One: uv run pytest -k test_get_lr_cosine_schedule passes. Two: build torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR with a lambda that calls my function divided by a_max, and SequentialLR(LinearLR(start_factor=1e-8, total_iters=T_w), CosineAnnealingLR(T_max=T_c-T_w, eta_min=a_min)); assert my values match the torch schedule to 1e-6 over every step after warmup, and explain the one-step offset in warmup.

10:30 MEASURE — Loss curves for warmup 0, 100, 300 overlaid, plus grad norm. Expected: no-warmup at high lr shows an early spike or plateau and ends worse; with warmup, smooth. Report final val loss for each.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Warmup protects the first steps when Adam's statistics are garbage; decay lets the model settle into a sharper minimum at the end. Interview line: 'The decay phase is where a lot of the final loss comes from, which is why WSD schedules can branch off checkpoints and decay late.'
12:00 NEXT — Next: Gradient clipping and stability
key_math: t < T_w: a = (t/T_w) a_max; T_w <= t <= T_c: a = a_min + 0.5(1 + cos(pi (t - T_w)/(T_c - T_w)))(a_max - a_min); t > T_c: a = a_min
code_task: get_lr_cosine_schedule(t, a_max, a_min, T_w, T_c) -> float; set param_group['lr'] each step; ablation script training the tiny GPT with warmup in {0, 100, 300}.
receipt: uv run pytest -k test_get_lr_cosine_schedule passes; post-warmup values match torch SequentialLR(LinearLR, CosineAnnealingLR(eta_min=a_min)) within 1e-6.
gotchas: Calling scheduler.step() before optimizer.step() shifts everything by one and PyTorch warns about it; Setting the lr once at construction and never updating param_groups, the plot looks right but training uses a constant lr; LinearLR start_factor must be > 0, so 'start from zero' needs a tiny factor or your own function
interview_q: Why do we use learning-rate warmup with Adam? Model answer: In the first steps Adam's second-moment estimate is based on very few gradients and the loss landscape is sharp, so full-size updates can blow up activations or push into a bad region. Ramping the lr up gives the statistics and the network time to stabilize.
explainer: We draw the learning rate as a curve over training steps. It starts at zero on the left.
For the first two hundred steps it climbs in a straight line. That ramp is the warmup.
At the top it hits the peak learning rate, then bends down along half a cosine wave.
The cosine ends at a floor, ten percent of peak, and stays flat there for the rest of training.
Next to it we show what Adam sees at step one: a variance estimate built from a single gradient.
Without the ramp, the very first update is full size, and the loss curve jumps right when it should be falling.
With the ramp, the loss slides down smoothly. Same model, same data, only the first two hundred steps changed.

Linear ramp segment drawn from 0 to a_max, shaded 'warmup'.
Half-cosine arc from a_max down, with cos formula written above.
Flat line at a_min labeled 0.1 x peak.
Inset: histogram of v estimate with one sample vs 200 samples.
Red loss curve with an early spike annotated 'no warmup'.
Green smooth loss curve overlaid; legend warmup=0 vs warmup=300.

hook: One bad batch can produce a gradient a thousand times bigger than normal. Clipping is the one line that stops it from wrecking your run.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — One bad batch can produce a gradient a thousand times bigger than normal. Clipping is the one line that stops it from wrecking your run.

0:15 QUESTION — Every big run log you have read, from OPT-175B to BLOOM, talks about loss spikes. Almost everyone clips the global gradient norm at 1.0. What exactly gets clipped, and why global instead of per-parameter?

1:00 INTUITION — Treat all the gradients in the model as one giant vector. If its length is over the limit, shrink the whole vector so its length equals the limit. Direction is untouched; only the step size is capped. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — total_norm = sqrt(sum over params p of ||g_p||_2^2). Note that is the L2 norm of all entries concatenated. clip_coef = max_norm / (total_norm + 1e-6). If clip_coef < 1: g_p <- g_p * clip_coef for every p. Per-parameter clipping would change the direction of the update; global clipping does not. Relation to Adam: Adam is roughly scale-invariant, so clipping mostly matters on the rare step where one batch dominates m and v.

4:30 CODE — def clip_grad_norm(params, max_norm, eps=1e-6): grads = [p.grad for p in params if p.grad is not None]; total = torch.sqrt(sum((g.detach().float()**2).sum() for g in grads)); coef = max_norm / (total + eps); if coef < 1: for g in grads: g.mul_(coef); return total. Log the pre-clip norm every step. Then inject a spike: on step 500 multiply one batch's loss by 1000, or feed a batch of one repeated token, with and without clipping.

8:00 RECEIPT — Clone grads, run mine on one copy and torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0) on the other. torch.testing.assert_close for every grad, and assert_close(my_total, torch_total). Then uv run pytest -k test_gradient_clipping.

9:30 MEASURE — Plot pre-clip grad norm over 1500 steps on log scale with the 1.0 line. Show what fraction of steps actually get clipped (often most early steps, few later). Then the injected spike: the unclipped run's loss jumps and takes hundreds of steps to recover; the clipped run barely notices.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — Clip the global norm, log it every step, and treat the grad-norm plot as your run's heart monitor. Interview line: 'A rising grad norm usually precedes a loss spike, so I alert on it rather than on loss.'
11:30 NEXT — Next: Mixed precision: fp32, fp16, bf16
key_math: ||g|| = sqrt(sum_p ||g_p||_2^2); c = max_norm / (||g|| + 1e-6); if c < 1: g_p <- c g_p
code_task: clip_grad_norm(params, max_norm, eps=1e-6) -> total_norm, in-place; training loop logs pre-clip norm; spike-injection experiment with and without clipping.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close on every grad and on the returned norm versus torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0); uv run pytest -k test_gradient_clipping passes.
gotchas: Clipping before loss.backward() finishes, or before gradient accumulation completes, clips a partial gradient; With fp16 GradScaler you must call scaler.unscale_(optimizer) before clipping or you clip scaled gradients; Computing the norm in bf16 loses precision on large models, accumulate in fp32
interview_q: Why clip the global gradient norm instead of each parameter's gradient separately? Model answer: Global clipping rescales all gradients by the same factor, so the update direction is preserved and only its magnitude is capped. Per-parameter clipping distorts the direction and changes the relative updates between layers.
explainer: We draw every gradient in the model as one long arrow in a high dimensional space, shown here in two dimensions.
Around the origin we draw a circle of radius one. That circle is the max norm.
On most steps, the gradient arrow lands comfortably inside the circle, and clipping leaves it completely alone.
Then a bad batch arrives and the arrow shoots far outside the circle, a thousand times too long.
We shrink it back along the same line until its tip touches the circle. Same direction, capped length.
Below, we watch the training loss without clipping jump sharply and take hundreds of steps to recover.
With clipping, the same bad batch is a tiny blip. That is why nearly every LLM clips at one.

hook: fp16 can't represent 70,000. bf16 can represent ten to the thirty-eight. That one fact is why every modern LLM trains in bf16.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — fp16 can't represent 70,000. bf16 can represent ten to the thirty-eight. That one fact is why every modern LLM trains in bf16.

0:15 QUESTION — Mixed precision is roughly a 2x speed and memory win, and it is how GPT-3 and Llama 3 were trained. But fp16 runs needed loss scaling and still diverged sometimes. What exactly is in the bits, and what stays in fp32?

1:00 INTUITION — A float is sign, exponent and mantissa. Exponent bits buy range, mantissa bits buy precision. fp16 spends bits on precision and runs out of range; bf16 keeps fp32's range and accepts coarse precision. Neural nets care about range far more. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — fp32: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa, max ~3.4e38, eps 1.2e-7. fp16: 1, 5, 10, max 65504, smallest normal 6.1e-5, eps 9.8e-4. bf16: 1, 8, 7, max ~3.4e38, eps 7.8e-3. Consequence one: small gradients underflow to zero in fp16, so Micikevicius et al. multiply the loss by S (e.g. 2^16), backprop, then divide grads by S. Consequence two: w + lr*g with lr*g below w*eps/2 rounds to w, so master weights and optimizer state stay fp32. Autocast runs matmuls in low precision and keeps reductions like softmax, norms and loss in fp32.

5:30 CODE — Show bits: torch.finfo(torch.float16), torch.finfo(torch.bfloat16). Demo: torch.tensor(70000.).half() is inf; torch.tensor(1e-8).half() is 0; torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.bfloat16) + 1e-3 is still 1.0. Training loop: with torch.autocast(device_type='mps', dtype=torch.bfloat16): logits = model(x); loss = F.cross_entropy(...). Params stay fp32. Print logits.dtype (bf16) and loss.dtype (fp32). fp16 path on CUDA: scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler('cuda'); scaler.scale(loss).backward(); scaler.unscale_(opt); clip; scaler.step(opt); scaler.update().

8:30 RECEIPT — Run the TinyStories GPT for 1000 steps in fp32 and in bf16 autocast with the same seed and batches. Check: final val loss within about 0.02 of fp32, and per-step loss curves overlap. Check on the M4 that your PyTorch version supports bf16 autocast on MPS; if it does not, run this episode's comparison on the RunPod 4090 with device_type='cuda'. Also show the fp16 failure: run without GradScaler and count steps where grads are all zero for some layer.

10:30 MEASURE — Table: tokens per second and peak memory for fp32 vs bf16 on the Mac (and on the 4090 if you have it up, where the gain is larger because tensor cores run bf16 at many times fp32 rate). Report val loss for each.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Use bf16 autocast, keep master weights and optimizer state in fp32, and you get the speed without loss scaling. Interview line: 'bf16 trades mantissa for exponent, so it has fp32's range, which removes the need for loss scaling.'

interview_q: Why does bf16 training usually not need loss scaling while fp16 does? Model answer: bf16 has 8 exponent bits like fp32, so small gradients do not underflow. fp16 has only 5 exponent bits and a smallest normal of about 6e-5, so gradients need to be scaled up to stay representable.
explainer: We lay out thirty two bits of a float32 in three colored groups: one sign bit, eight exponent bits, twenty three mantissa bits.
Exponent bits set how big or small a number can get. Mantissa bits set how finely we can step between numbers.
Now fp16. It keeps ten mantissa bits but only five exponent bits, so it tops out at sixty five thousand.
bf16 simply chops fp32's mantissa down to seven bits. The exponent stays eight bits, so the range is the same as fp32.
We plot a histogram of real gradients on a log scale. In fp16 the left tail falls off a cliff and becomes zero.
Loss scaling slides the whole histogram right by multiplying by sixty five thousand, then slides it back after.
With bf16 the histogram already fits. That is why modern training just uses bf16 autocast with fp32 master weights.

hook: Want a batch of half a million tokens on a laptop? Run sixteen small batches, add the gradients, and step once. The math is identical.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Want a batch of half a million tokens on a laptop? Run sixteen small batches, add the gradients, and step once. The math is identical.
0:15 QUESTION — GPT-3 small used a batch of 0.5M tokens. nanoGPT reproduces GPT-2 with total_batch_size = 524288 tokens even on one GPU. How, when only a few thousand tokens fit in memory?

1:00 INTUITION — The gradient of an average is the average of the gradients. So split the big batch into micro-batches, backprop each one, and let PyTorch sum the grads into .grad. Divide by the number of micro-batches and you have the big-batch gradient. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Big batch of size B = k*b: L = (1/B) sum_i l_i. Grad: dL/dw = (1/k) sum_{j=1..k} [(1/b) sum_{i in micro j} dl_i/dw]. So loss_micro / k, backward k times, PyTorch accumulates. Caveat: if micro-batches have different numbers of valid (non-padded) tokens, the mean-of-means is wrong; divide the summed loss by the total token count instead. Cost: same FLOPs, k times the wall-clock per step, memory of one micro-batch.

4:30 CODE — accum_steps = total_batch // (B*T). Loop: opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True); for micro in range(accum_steps): x, y = get_batch(...); with autocast: loss = model(x, y) / accum_steps; loss.backward(). Then clip_grad_norm, opt.step(). Show nanoGPT's version and its DDP detail: model.require_backward_grad_sync = (micro == accum_steps - 1), which is the same idea as the no_sync() context manager.

7:30 RECEIPT — Fixed batch X of shape (32, 128). Model A: one backward on all 32 rows. Model B, same weights: four backwards on 8-row slices with loss/4. For every parameter: torch.testing.assert_close(pA.grad, pB.grad, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6) in float32, and exact-ish in float64. Then the padded case: make one micro-batch half padding with ignore_index=-100 and show the naive /k version fails the check and the token-count version passes.

9:30 MEASURE — Max abs grad difference: float32 vs float64 (tiny, from summation order). Then train 500 steps with effective batch 64 two ways (one batch of 64 vs 8 micro-batches of 8) and overlay loss curves; plus peak memory of each.

10:30 TAKEAWAY — Gradient accumulation trades time for memory with exactly the same math, as long as you normalize by the right count. Interview line: 'Accumulation is exact for mean losses with equal token counts; with variable lengths you normalize by total tokens, not by number of micro-batches.'
11:00 NEXT — Next: Checkpointing and resumable training
key_math: grad L_B = (1/k) sum_{j=1..k} grad L_{b_j} for B = k b with equal-size micro-batches; variable lengths: L = (sum of token losses) / (total valid tokens)
code_task: train_step(model, opt, get_batch, accum_steps) with loss / accum_steps and a single optimizer step; equivalence test comparing grads from one 32-row batch vs four 8-row micro-batches; padded variant normalizing by total tokens.
receipt: For all params: torch.testing.assert_close(grad_big_batch, grad_accumulated, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6) in float32 (exact to ~1e-12 in float64).
gotchas: Forgetting to divide by accum_steps gives k times the gradient, AdamW mostly hides it but clipping and SGD do not; Calling zero_grad inside the micro loop throws away all but the last micro-batch; Dropout or BatchNorm make the comparison fail for real reasons, turn dropout off for the test
interview_q: Is gradient accumulation exactly equivalent to a larger batch? Model answer: For a mean loss over equal-sized micro-batches without batch-dependent layers, yes up to floating-point summation order. It breaks with BatchNorm, with variable valid-token counts unless you renormalize, and with different dropout masks.
explainer: We see one big batch of thirty two rows that is too tall to fit in our memory box.
We slice it into four strips of eight rows. Each strip fits in the box on its own.
Strip one goes forward and backward. Its gradient lands in a bucket labeled dot grad.
Strips two, three and four do the same. Their gradients pour into the same bucket and add up.
Each strip's loss was divided by four, so the bucket now holds the average, exactly the big-batch gradient.
Only now does the optimizer take one step, and the bucket is emptied for the next round.
Side by side, the big-batch gradient and the accumulated gradient match to six decimal places.

hook: I killed my training run at step 600 and resumed it. The loss curve after resume is identical to the one that never stopped.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — I killed my training run at step 600 and resumed it. The loss curve after resume is identical to the one that never stopped.

0:15 QUESTION — Big runs crash constantly; the Llama 3 paper reports hundreds of interruptions over its 54-day pretraining. If resume is not exact, you cannot tell a real loss spike from a checkpoint bug. What has to be saved besides the weights?

1:00 INTUITION — A training run is a state machine. The state is the weights, the optimizer's m and v, the step counter that drives the lr schedule and bias correction, and the random number generators that pick batches and dropout masks. Save all four or you resume a different run. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Why each piece matters: lose m, v and the AdamW step counter and bias correction restarts at t=1, so the first steps after resume are effectively a fresh high-lr warmup-less update. Lose the step and the schedule restarts warmup. Lose the RNG and you see different batches, so the curve diverges in noise even if the model is fine. Size: fp32 weights 4 bytes/param plus m and v 8 bytes/param, so a checkpoint is about 3x the model.

4:30 CODE — def save_checkpoint(model, optimizer, iteration, out): torch.save({'model': model.state_dict(), 'optimizer': optimizer.state_dict(), 'iteration': iteration, 'torch_rng': torch.get_rng_state(), 'mps_rng': torch.mps.get_rng_state() if on MPS, 'numpy_rng': np.random.get_state(), 'python_rng': random.getstate()}, out). Write to out + '.tmp' then os.replace for atomicity. def load_checkpoint(src, model, optimizer) -> iteration: ckpt = torch.load(src, weights_only=False) (your own trusted file), load_state_dict both, restore RNGs, return ckpt['iteration']. Unwrap torch.compile's _orig_mod prefix if present.

8:00 RECEIPT — Run A: 1000 steps straight on CPU, deterministic, log loss per step. Run B: 600 steps, save, delete the model and optimizer objects, start a new process, load, run to 1000. assert losses_A[600:] == losses_B[600:] exactly on CPU (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)); on MPS use allclose with atol 1e-5. Also uv run pytest -k test_checkpointing.

10:00 MEASURE — Overlay curves A and B: they lie on top of each other. Then the broken version that saves only model.state_dict(): plot the jump at step 600. Report checkpoint size on disk vs parameter count times 12 bytes.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — Checkpoint everything that changes: weights, optimizer state, step, RNGs, and data position. Interview line: 'I test resumability by checking the resumed loss curve is bitwise identical to an uninterrupted run, so infra bugs never look like optimization problems.'

key_math: checkpoint bytes ~= 4N (weights) + 8N (Adam m, v) = 12N for fp32; bias correction 1/(1-b^t) depends on saved t
code_task: save_checkpoint(model, optimizer, iteration, out) and load_checkpoint(src, model, optimizer) -> iteration, saving model/optimizer state_dicts, step, and torch/numpy/python RNG states with atomic write.
receipt: Losses of an uninterrupted 1000-step CPU run equal losses of a 600 + resume-to-1000 run exactly (deterministic mode); CS336 uv run pytest -k test_checkpointing passes.
gotchas: torch.load defaults to weights_only=True since PyTorch 2.6, so pickled numpy RNG state fails to load unless you pass weights_only=False for your own files; Saving a torch.compile'd model gives '_orig_mod.' prefixed keys that do not load into the plain model; Creating the optimizer before moving the model to the device, then loading state, leaves m and v on the wrong device
interview_q: What do you need to save to resume LLM training exactly? Model answer: Model weights, full optimizer state including step counts, the lr scheduler or step number, all RNG states, and the data loader position. Missing any of them changes the trajectory, and missing optimizer state can cause a loss spike on resume.
explainer: We see a training run as a box with four dials inside: weights, optimizer moments, step counter, and random seed.
The loss curve draws itself as the run goes. At step six hundred, we pull the plug.
First we save only the weights. On resume, the moments reset to zero and the step counter reads one.
The loss curve jumps right at step six hundred. The model was fine. The checkpoint was not.
Now we save all four dials into the file and write it atomically, temp file first, then rename.
On resume, every dial snaps back to where it was. The new curve traces exactly over the old one.
The difference plot between the two runs is a flat line at zero. That is a correct checkpoint.

Loss curve drawing left to right; a plug icon pulled at step 600.

Loss curve with a visible jump at 600, red annotation 'checkpoint bug'.

Two curves A and B overlapping exactly after step 600.
Flat zero line labeled 'losses_A - losses_B'.

hook: The same model can sound brilliant or broken depending on four lines of sampling code. Let's write all four and watch it happen.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The same model can sound brilliant or broken depending on four lines of sampling code. Let's write all four and watch it happen.

0:15 QUESTION — Every API, from OpenAI's to Anthropic's, exposes temperature and top_p. Holtzman et al. showed that greedy and beam search produce repetitive text, and pure sampling produces nonsense. Where exactly does each method fail?

1:00 INTUITION — The model gives you a probability bar chart for the next token. Greedy always takes the tallest bar. Temperature stretches or flattens the chart. Top-k keeps the k tallest bars. Top-p keeps the smallest set of bars whose heights add up to p. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — p_i = softmax(z / tau)_i. tau -> 0 is greedy, tau = 1 is the model, tau > 1 flattens. Top-k: set z_i = -inf for all but the top k, renormalize. Top-p: sort p descending, cumulative sum c; keep tokens with c_i - p_i < p (so the token that crosses p is kept), renormalize. Show why top-k is brittle: a flat distribution needs k = 500, a peaked one needs k = 2, and top-p adapts automatically.

5:00 CODE — def sample(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None, generator=None): logits (B, V) from the last position. if temperature == 0: return argmax. logits = logits / temperature. top_k: v, _ = torch.topk(logits, k); logits[logits < v[:, [-1]]] = -inf. top_p: sorted, idx = logits.sort(descending=True); probs = sorted.softmax(-1); cum = probs.cumsum(-1); remove = cum - probs > top_p; sorted[remove] = -inf; scatter back. torch.multinomial(F.softmax(logits, -1), 1, generator=generator). generate(model, prompt_ids, max_new_tokens) loops with context cropping to T.

8:30 RECEIPT — Compare my filtered logits to Hugging Face's logits processors: transformers TemperatureLogitsWarper(0.8), TopKLogitsWarper(top_k=50), TopPLogitsWarper(top_p=0.9) applied to the same logits. Assert torch.equal(torch.isinf(mine), torch.isinf(hf)) and assert_close on the finite entries. Also assert temperature=0 output equals logits.argmax(-1).

10:00 MEASURE — Side by side on the TinyStories model, same prompt, same seed: greedy (repetition loop), tau=1.5 (gibberish), top-k 40, top-p 0.9. Quantify: distinct-2 (unique bigrams / total bigrams) and repetition rate for 50 samples each, in a table.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Greedy repeats, high temperature hallucinates words, top-p trims the unreliable tail adaptively. Interview line: 'Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens covering p of the mass, so it adapts to how confident the model is, which top-k cannot.'

hook: One line, torch.compile, and my GPT trains faster. Not because of magic, because it stopped writing the same tensor to memory five times.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — One line, torch.compile, and my GPT trains faster. Not because of magic, because it stopped writing the same tensor to memory five times.

0:15 QUESTION — nanoGPT, the speedrun and torchtitan all wrap the model in torch.compile. Horace He's 'Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr' explains why: most deep learning ops are memory-bound, not compute-bound. What does compile actually do, and when does it not help?

1:00 INTUITION — Eager PyTorch is a cook who walks to the fridge for every ingredient, one at a time. A fused kernel grabs everything in one trip, does all the chopping at the counter, and puts the dish back once. Same work, far fewer trips. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Take y = gelu(x * w + b) on a tensor of n elements in fp32. Eager: mul reads 2n writes n, add reads 2n writes n, gelu reads n writes n, about 8n * 4 bytes of traffic. Fused: read x, w, b once, write y once, about 4n * 4 bytes, often less with broadcast. Time for a memory-bound op ~ bytes / bandwidth, so fusion can approach the ratio of traffic. Compile pipeline: TorchDynamo captures an FX graph from Python bytecode, AOTAutograd builds the joint forward and backward graph, TorchInductor emits fused Triton (GPU) or C++ (CPU) kernels.

5:30 CODE — model = torch.compile(model). Time it: first call includes compile (seconds to minutes). Benchmark tokens/s over 50 steps after 10 warmup steps, eager vs compiled. Show a graph break: put print(x.shape) or a .item() inside forward and run with TORCH_LOGS='graph_breaks'. Use torch._dynamo.explain(model)(x) to count graphs and breaks. Try mode='max-autotune' and compare. Note: run on the Mac first; MPS support in Inductor is newer, so if it graph-breaks or gives no gain, run the same script on the RunPod 4090, which is where the next module lives anyway.

9:00 RECEIPT — Correctness: torch.testing.assert_close(compiled(x), eager(x), rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4) for logits, and the training loss of 200 compiled steps tracks the eager curve. Speed: compare your speedup to nanoGPT's README note that compile cut iteration time from about 250 ms to 135 ms on its setup. You will not match their number on different hardware; report yours honestly.

11:00 MEASURE — Bar chart: tokens/s eager vs compile vs max-autotune, and compile time in seconds. Profiler kernel count per step, eager vs compiled (number of CUDA or Metal kernels launched), which is the clearest evidence of fusion.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Compile wins by fusing memory-bound ops and cutting launch overhead; graph breaks quietly give it all back. Interview line: 'I check graph breaks with TORCH_LOGS and count kernels in the profiler before I trust a compile speedup.' M07E17 opens up the generated Triton.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Experiment tracking and ablations
key_math: t_memory-bound ~= bytes_moved / bandwidth; eager y=gelu(xw+b): ~8n reads+writes vs fused ~4n; speedup <= traffic_eager / traffic_fused
code_task: bench_tokens_per_s(model, steps=50, warmup=10) for eager, torch.compile(model), torch.compile(model, mode='max-autotune'); graph-break demo with TORCH_LOGS='graph_breaks' and torch._dynamo.explain.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(compiled_model(x), model(x), rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4); measured speedup reported next to nanoGPT's published ~250 ms -> ~135 ms per iteration note.
gotchas: Timing the first compiled call measures compilation, not the kernel; .item(), print and data-dependent Python control flow inside forward cause graph breaks; Changing input shapes every step triggers recompiles, use fixed T or mark dynamic
interview_q: Why does torch.compile speed up a transformer even though matmuls are already cuBLAS? Model answer: The matmuls are not where compile helps much. It fuses the many memory-bound elementwise and normalization ops around them into fewer kernels, cutting memory traffic and kernel launch overhead.
explainer: We see a GPU as two places: a huge slow warehouse called HBM, and a tiny fast workbench where compute happens.
Eager PyTorch runs multiply, then add, then GELU. Each op hauls the tensor from the warehouse to the bench and back.
Three ops means three round trips. The arrows between warehouse and bench pile up, and the compute units mostly wait.
torch.compile looks at the whole graph first. It sees the three ops touch the same data.
Inductor writes one fused kernel. The tensor goes to the bench once, all three ops run there, and it goes back once.
The traffic counter drops by about half. For memory-bound ops, time drops right along with it.
But one print statement inside forward splits the graph in two, and the fusion across that line is lost.

Arrow count = 6 trips; compute icons show idle 'zzz'.
An FX graph of three nodes highlighted together.
One arrow in, three ops on the bench, one arrow out; label 'fused kernel'.
Bytes-moved counter animates from 8n to 4n.
Graph split by a red 'print()' node into two kernels.

The kernel count drop is the clearest evidence of fusion. I also triggered and fixed graph breaks, which explained a speedup I had lost without noticing.

hook: Most of my 'improvements' disappeared when I reran them with a second seed. Here is how to run ablations that survive.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Most of my 'improvements' disappeared when I reran them with a second seed. Here is how to run ablations that survive.

0:15 QUESTION — Research engineers at labs spend most of their time on controlled comparisons, not big runs. The CS336 assignments ask you to ablate learning rate, batch size and architecture. How do you know a 0.02 loss difference is real?

1:00 INTUITION — An ablation is a lab experiment. Change one knob, hold everything else fixed, including the data order and token budget, and repeat with a few seeds so you can see the noise floor. If the effect is smaller than the seed-to-seed spread, it is not an effect. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Noise floor: run the same config with s seeds, get val losses L_1..L_s, mean and std. Standard error = std / sqrt(s). Two configs differ meaningfully if |mean_A - mean_B| is several standard errors apart. Fixed compute: compare at equal tokens (and, for size changes, equal FLOPs 6ND), not equal steps. LR is the knob that interacts with everything, so each width or depth gets its own small LR sweep, otherwise you are comparing a tuned model with a mistuned one.

5:00 CODE — wandb.init(project='llm-first-principles', config=vars(args), group='m06e12-width'). wandb.log({'train/loss':..., 'val/loss':..., 'lr':..., 'grad_norm':..., 'tokens_per_s':...}, step=step). Sweep runner: for d_model in [128, 256, 384]: for n_layers in [2, 4, 6]: for lr in [1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2]: for seed in [0, 1, 2]: launch run with fixed token budget. Same data seed for all, separate model-init seed. If you prefer no account, log to CSV and plot with pandas; wandb offline mode also works.

8:30 RECEIPT — Two checks. One: seed noise floor, same config 3 seeds, std of final val loss reported (expect around 0.01 at this scale). Two: the published direction. CS336 and the Kaplan paper both say loss improves with model size at fixed data, and that the best LR shrinks as width grows. Assert your sweep reproduces both directions; if it does not, find out why before moving on.

10:30 MEASURE — Heatmap: final val loss over (width, LR) at fixed depth, each cell mean of 3 seeds with std annotated. Line plot: best LR vs width. Table: what moved loss most (usually LR choice and model size), what barely did.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Fix the token budget, sweep LR per config, use seeds, and report the noise floor next to every delta. Interview line: 'I only call an ablation a win if it beats the seed-to-seed standard error at matched compute.' This discipline is what P5 is graded on.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Scaling laws: Kaplan vs Chinchilla
key_math: SE = std(L_1..L_s) / sqrt(s); effect real if |mu_A - mu_B| >> sqrt(SE_A^2 + SE_B^2); compare at fixed D or fixed C = 6ND
code_task: sweep.py launching the TinyStories trainer over d_model x n_layers x lr x seed at a fixed token budget, logging to wandb (or CSV); analysis notebook producing heatmaps with mean +/- std.
receipt: Seed noise floor (std over 3 seeds) reported; sweep reproduces the published directions: larger model -> lower loss at fixed tokens, and optimal LR decreasing with width.
gotchas: Comparing runs at equal steps when batch sizes differ, compare at equal tokens; Reusing one data seed for model init and data order, so you cannot separate the two noise sources; Declaring a winner from one seed when the delta is inside the noise
interview_q: You changed the architecture and val loss dropped 0.015. Do you ship it? Model answer: Not yet. I would check the seed-to-seed spread at this scale, rerun both with 3+ seeds at matched tokens and a tuned LR for each, and only call it real if the gap is several standard errors.
explainer: We see two loss curves, config A and config B. B ends slightly lower, and it looks like a win.
Now we rerun A with two more seeds. Three A curves fan out into a band.
We do the same for B. Its band overlaps A's band almost completely. The win was noise.
Next we draw a grid. Rows are model width, columns are learning rate, each cell colored by final loss.
The best cell in each row slides left as width grows. Wider models want smaller learning rates.
If we had used one learning rate for every row, the wide model would look worse than it really is.
So every ablation gets three things: matched tokens, its own learning-rate sweep, and error bars.

Checklist card: matched tokens, lr sweep, 3 seeds.

hook: Kaplan said make models bigger. Chinchilla said train longer. Ten lines of Python on the published fit give twenty tokens per parameter.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Kaplan said make models bigger. Chinchilla said train longer. Ten lines of Python on the published fit give twenty tokens per parameter.

0:15 QUESTION — Gopher was 280B parameters on 300B tokens. Chinchilla, 70B on 1.4T tokens with the same compute, beat it on almost everything. Why did the two scaling-law papers disagree, and where does 20 tokens per parameter come from?

1:00 INTUITION — You have a fixed compute budget, C = 6ND. Spend it on a bigger model or on more data. Loss has a part that shrinks with N and a part that shrinks with D, plus a floor you can never beat. The optimum balances the two shrinking parts. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Kaplan 2020: L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N with alpha_N ~ 0.076, L(D) ~ D^-0.095, and compute-optimal N_opt ~ C^0.73, so most extra compute goes into parameters. Chinchilla 2022 parametric fit: L(N, D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta, published E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, alpha = 0.34, beta = 0.28. Minimize subject to C = 6ND: substitute D = C/(6N), set dL/dN = 0, giving N_opt = G (C/6)^(beta/(alpha+beta)), so N_opt ~ C^a with a = beta/(alpha+beta). Their three approaches gave a ~ 0.46 to 0.5, meaning N and D grow equally. Why Kaplan differed: fixed LR schedule length across runs, small models, and non-embedding parameter counts.

6:00 CODE — def chinchilla_loss(N, D, E, A, B, alpha, beta). def optimal_N(C, params): grid N over logspace(6, 13, 100000), D = C/(6N), argmin loss. Run for C in [1e19, 1e21, 5.76e23] with the paper's fit and with the Epoch AI refit from Besiroglu et al. 2024 (E = 1.82, A = 482.01, B = 2085.43, alpha = 0.3478, beta = 0.3658). Print N, D, D/N.

8:30 RECEIPT — With the Epoch refit, at Chinchilla's compute 5.76e23 the optimizer returns about N = 7e10 and D = 1.3e12, D/N about 18, and D/N stays near 20 (about 24 at 1e19, 22 at 1e21). That matches Chinchilla's actual 70B / 1.4T model. With the paper's printed Approach 3 fit, D/N drifts from about 32 to about 93, which is exactly the inconsistency Epoch's replication pointed out. Assert 15 < D/N < 30 for the refit at all three budgets.

10:30 MEASURE — Plot IsoFLOP curves: loss vs N for three compute budgets, minima marked, and the line through the minima on log-log axes with its slope (about 0.5). Overlay the Kaplan exponent 0.73 for contrast.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Compute-optimal training scales params and tokens together, about 20 tokens per parameter; modern models overtrain far past that on purpose because inference cost matters too. Interview line: 'Chinchilla is compute-optimal for training only; Llama 3 8B saw 15T tokens, almost 2000 per parameter, because a smaller model is cheaper to serve.'
12:00 NEXT — Next: Fit your own scaling law
key_math: C ~= 6ND; L(N,D) = E + A N^-alpha + B D^-beta; N_opt ∝ C^(beta/(alpha+beta)), D_opt ∝ C^(alpha/(alpha+beta)); Kaplan: N_opt ∝ C^0.73
code_task: chinchilla_loss(N, D, E, A, B, alpha, beta); optimal_N(C, params) via grid search over log N with D = C/(6N); IsoFLOP plot for three budgets with both the paper and Epoch-refit parameters.
receipt: Epoch refit (E=1.82, A=482.01, B=2085.43, alpha=0.3478, beta=0.3658) gives N_opt ~7e10, D_opt ~1.3e12 (D/N ~18) at C=5.76e23, matching Chinchilla's 70B/1.4T; assert 15 < D/N < 30 at C in {1e19, 1e21, 5.76e23}.
gotchas: Using C = 2ND (forward only) instead of 6ND shifts every answer by 3x; Mixing Kaplan's non-embedding parameter counts with Chinchilla's total counts; Reading 20 tokens/param as a universal law, it depends on the fit and drifts with the paper's own Approach 3 numbers
interview_q: If you get 4x more compute, how should you split it between model size and data under Chinchilla? Model answer: Roughly equally in exponent: about 2x more parameters and 2x more tokens, since N_opt and D_opt both scale close to C^0.5. Kaplan's laws would have put most of it into parameters.
explainer: We draw a budget of compute as a fixed rectangle. Its area is six times parameters times tokens.
We can make the rectangle tall and thin, a huge model on little data, or short and wide, a tiny model on lots of data.
For each shape we compute the loss. Plotted against model size, the losses trace a U shaped valley.
The bottom of the valley is the compute optimal model for this budget. We mark it with a dot.
We repeat for a bigger budget and a smaller one. Three valleys, three dots, moving right and down.
On log axes the dots fall on a straight line. Its slope is about one half, so parameters and tokens grow together.
At Chinchilla's budget the dot lands at seventy billion parameters and about one point four trillion tokens.

hook: I trained six tiny GPTs on my laptop and fit a straight line. It predicted the seventh model's loss before I trained it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — I trained six tiny GPTs on my laptop and fit a straight line. It predicted the seventh model's loss before I trained it.

0:15 QUESTION — Labs decide whether to spend millions on a run by fitting scaling laws on small models first; the GPT-4 report says they predicted final loss from runs with 1000x less compute. CS336 Assignment 3 is entirely about this. Can we do a tiny version honestly on a Mac?

1:00 INTUITION — Train models of six sizes at a fixed, generous token budget. Plot final loss against parameters on log-log axes. If it is a power law plus a floor, the points bend onto a curve you can fit with three numbers, then extrapolate. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Model: L(N) = E + A N^(-alpha). Taking logs of (L - E) makes it linear: log(L - E) = log A - alpha log N. Fit with nonlinear least squares in log space: minimize sum_i (log L_i - log(E + A N_i^-alpha))^2. Hold out the largest model; fit on the other five or six; predict it. Also the compute view: L vs C = 6ND across runs at different durations. Explain why non-embedding N is used at this scale: embeddings are a huge fraction of a tiny model and distort the fit.

5:00 CODE — sizes: d_model in [64, 96, 128, 192, 256, 384] with depth scaled (e.g. n_layers 2 to 6), heads = d_model // 32. Same tokenizer, same data order, fixed tokens (e.g. 50M), LR tuned per size from a 3-point sweep. Count N_nonembed = sum of p.numel() excluding token embedding and LM head. Fit: scipy.optimize.curve_fit(lambda logN, logA, alpha, E: np.log(E + np.exp(logA) * np.exp(logN)**(-alpha)), logN, logL, p0=[...], bounds=...). Bootstrap over points for an alpha confidence interval.

8:30 RECEIPT — Two checks. One: prediction. Train a seventh, larger model (e.g. d_model 512) only after fitting; assert |predicted - actual| < 0.05 in val loss, and show it on screen. Two: published exponent. Compare your alpha to Kaplan's alpha_N ~ 0.076 and Chinchilla's alpha ~ 0.34. Explain why yours will not equal either: different data (TinyStories is far simpler than web text), fixed tokens rather than converged, and a fitted floor E. The test is the prediction, not matching their exponent.

10:30 MEASURE — Log-log plot: six points, fitted curve, the held-out seventh point with its predicted value as an open circle and its actual as a filled circle. Annotate alpha with the bootstrap 95 percent interval and E.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — A scaling law is only useful if it predicts a run you have not done yet; always hold one out. Interview line: 'I fit L = E + A N^-alpha on small runs with per-size LR tuning and validated it by predicting a held-out larger model within 0.05 loss.'
12:00 NEXT — Next: Data quality: filtering and dedup
key_math: L(N) = E + A N^-alpha; fit min_theta sum_i (log L_i - log(E + A N_i^-alpha))^2; predict L(N_7) before training it
code_task: scaling_sweep.py training 6 GPT sizes at fixed tokens with a small per-size LR sweep; fit_power_law(N, L) -> (E, A, alpha) via scipy.optimize.curve_fit in log space; bootstrap CI; held-out 7th model.
receipt: Held-out larger model's actual val loss within 0.05 of the fitted law's prediction made before training; fitted alpha reported with 95% bootstrap CI alongside Kaplan 0.076 and Chinchilla 0.34 with the reasons they differ.
gotchas: Using one LR for all sizes bends the curve, because small models are under-tuned or large ones diverge; Counting embedding parameters in tiny models makes the fit meaningless; Fitting a pure power law with no floor E when the smallest losses approach the data's entropy
interview_q: How would you decide if a 10x bigger training run is worth it? Model answer: Fit a scaling law on a ladder of smaller runs with tuned hyperparameters, validate it by predicting a held-out run, then extrapolate the loss to the big run and weigh the predicted gain against the compute cost.
explainer: We start with an empty log log plot. The horizontal axis is parameter count, the vertical is validation loss.
Six dots drop in one at a time, one for each tiny model we trained on the laptop.
They do not lie on a straight line. They bend, flattening toward a floor we call E.
We subtract the floor, and now the dots line up straight. The slope of that line is minus alpha.
We extend the fitted curve to the right, into a model size we have not trained yet, and mark the prediction.
Now we train that seventh model. Its real loss drops in right next to the predicted circle.
That is what a scaling law is for. Small, cheap runs telling us what the expensive run will do.

hook: The same web page appears thousands of times in Common Crawl. MinHash finds the near-copies in linear time, and it fits in forty lines.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The same web page appears thousands of times in Common Crawl. MinHash finds the near-copies in linear time, and it fits in forty lines.

0:15 QUESTION — FineWeb, the dataset modded-nanogpt trains on, is Common Crawl after heuristic filters and MinHash deduplication, and the FineWeb team showed each step measurably improves downstream scores. Comparing every pair of a billion documents is impossible. How does MinHash avoid it?

1:00 INTUITION — Turn each document into a set of word 5-grams. Jaccard similarity is overlap over union. MinHash is a magic fingerprint: the chance two documents share one minimum hash value equals their Jaccard similarity. Locality sensitive hashing groups the fingerprints into buckets so only likely duplicates ever get compared. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. For a random hash h, P[min h(A) = min h(B)] = J(A, B), because the minimum over the union is equally likely to be any element, and it matches only if it is in the intersection. With k hash functions, J_hat = (matches)/k, std = sqrt(J(1-J)/k). LSH: split k into b bands of r rows; a pair becomes a candidate if any band matches fully. P(candidate) = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b, an S-curve. FineWeb used 112 hashes as 14 bands of 8, which puts the steep part around 0.75 similarity.

Candidates -> verify with exact Jaccard -> union-find clusters. Also three heuristic filters from the FineWeb/Gopher rules: too-short docs, high fraction of lines ending without punctuation, high symbol-to-word ratio.

interview_q: How would you deduplicate a trillion-token web corpus? Model answer: Exact dedup with hashes for identical documents, then near-dup with MinHash over word n-grams plus LSH banding so only bucket collisions are compared, then union-find to pick one per cluster. Tune bands and rows to set the similarity threshold, and check the effect on downstream evals rather than assuming more dedup is better.
explainer: We see two web pages that are almost the same. Below each, their word five grams spill out as small cards.
The cards they share light up in the middle. Jaccard similarity is the shared cards over all cards.
Now we apply a random hash to every card and keep only the smallest value from each page.
Those two minimums match exactly when the smallest card overall is a shared one. The chance of that is the Jaccard similarity.
We repeat with one hundred twelve hashes and get a fingerprint of one hundred twelve numbers per page.
We cut the fingerprint into fourteen bands of eight. Pages that match on any full band fall into the same bucket.
The probability of sharing a bucket traces an S curve that rises sharply near seventy five percent similarity.
So we never compare all pairs. We hash every page once and only check the pages that land together.

interview_q: What is Muon and why does it help? Model answer: Muon takes SGD-momentum updates for 2D weight matrices and replaces each with an approximately orthogonal matrix via Newton-Schulz iterations, so the update has equal magnitude along all singular directions instead of being dominated by a few. It cut speedrun time substantially and is applied only to hidden matrices, with AdamW for embeddings, head and scalars.

Newton Schulz iterations squeeze those singular values toward one. After five steps they all sit in a band around one.
Now every direction in the matrix gets a similar sized step. That is the whole idea behind Muon.
